result.summary: Venus, wounded by Cupid's arrow, falls in love with Adonis and follows him hunting, warning him against dangerous beasts. Resting under a poplar, she tells how Hippomenes won Atalanta in a race with her golden apples, then forgot to thank her and was turned with Atalanta into lions for profaning Cybele's shrine.

scenes.title: Venus loves Adonis and warns him
scenes.summary: Grazed by Cupid's arrow, Venus abandons her favorite haunts to follow Adonis hunting. She warns him against fierce beasts and draws him down to rest under a poplar.
scenes.stakes: Venus fears losing Adonis to the wild beasts he might rashly attack.

scenes.title: Atalanta's race and Hippomenes' challenge
scenes.summary: Atalanta, warned by the oracle, kills suitors who lose her race. Hippomenes first scorns them, then is struck by her beauty and offers to race her.
scenes.stakes: Hippomenes risks death if he loses; Atalanta fears the oracle's prophecy of ruin through marriage.

scenes.title: Atalanta's doubts
scenes.summary: Atalanta pities Hippomenes and wishes he would withdraw, falling in love without realizing it.
scenes.stakes: Atalanta faces guilt over a youth's death and the oracle's warning.

scenes.title: The golden apples win the race
scenes.summary: Hippomenes prays to Venus, who gives him three golden apples from Cyprus. He throws them to delay Atalanta and wins.
scenes.stakes: Hippomenes' life and his chance to win Atalanta.

scenes.title: Ingratitude and transformation into lions
scenes.summary: Slighted by Hippomenes, Venus makes him desire Atalanta in Cybele's shrine. Cybele turns them into lions, and Venus warns Adonis again.
scenes.stakes: Hippomenes and Atalanta suffer divine punishment for sacrilege; Venus fears for Adonis.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet from the island of Cythera, linked with her cult.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous reflection on the swift passing of time, introducing Adonis.
Echoes the proverb that fortune or the divine favors the bold.

analysis.text: Passion overrides reason and piety, as Cupid's arrow, Atalanta's love and Hippomenes' lust show. Gratitude owed to the gods and respect for sacred places have deadly consequences.
Venus's tale foreshadows Adonis's death by a boar: she warns him of beasts, yet he will not heed her.

legacy.text: The race with golden apples became a classic motif in art and literature, painted by Guido Reni (c. 1618–19) among others.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's version makes Hippomenes' lion transformation a punishment, whereas other ancient sources have Atalanta's husband sometimes named Melanion.

language_notes.text: Adonis was born of Myrrha and her father Cinyras; Myrrha was turned into a myrrh tree, from which he was born. So he is child of his sister and grandfather in effect.
The 'flames of his mother' refers to Myrrha's incestuous passion, which Venus had caused; Adonis, as Myrrha's son, now becomes Venus's own torment.
Cytherian shores, Paphos, Cnidos and Amathus were centres of Venus's worship, so abandoning them shows how complete her devotion to Adonis has become.
'Robes tucked up after the manner of Diana' means dressed for hunting like the huntress goddess, with skirts gathered to the knee.
'Lightning in their curving tusks' means the boar's tusks strike with sudden, deadly force, like a thunderbolt.
The oracle's warning is the traditional ambiguous prophecy: marriage will somehow ruin her. It sets up her eventual transformation, which the reader may know from the myth.
The speaker, Venus, addresses Adonis, her beloved, whose beauty was proverbial. She is telling this tale to him, so the comparison is personal.
Aonian means Boeotian, from Aonia, a part of Boeotia in Greece; it identifies Hippomenes' homeland. The Scythians were famed archers, so their arrows signify great speed.
Pinions here means the fluttering ends of her garments, likened to wings; the leggings are decorated bands worn below the knee.
Hippomenes claims descent from Neptune, god of the sea, through Onchestius and Megareus, to impress Atalanta with his lineage.
Daughter of Schœneus is Atalanta. Her father's name marks her as the swift huntress who races her suitors and kills those she beats.
The monarch of the sea is Neptune; Hippomenes is his great-grandson. Atalanta counts this noble descent among his merits.
Impelled onwards to weariness of life means he is driven to be tired of living, that is, to court death recklessly.
A feminine look means a delicate, beardless, girlish face. She sees youthful softness and so pities him all the more.
Vexatious Divinities refers to the gods who, by an oracle, forbade her to marry. Her complaint hints at that prophecy.
Cytherea is a name for Venus, taken from the island of Cythera, near which she was said to have risen from the sea. Venus is the speaker here.
Tamasenian field: a plain at Tamasus in Cyprus, an island sacred to Venus. The footnote marks the place name.
The runners are said to be so light they could cross the sea or the tops of the grain without wetting their feet or bending the ears.
The Megarean hero is Hippomenes, who came from Megara. The virgin daughter of Schœneus is Atalanta.
Thrown in an oblique direction means off to the side, so Atalanta must run farther out of her way to fetch it.
Venus means she will shorten the story so that it is not slower than the race itself.

context_notes.text: Venus's son is Cupid, whose arrows cause love; here his arrow accidentally wounds his own mother.
Diana was the virgin goddess of the hunt, a figure very unlike Venus, goddess of love.
Losing suitors were put to death, yet many still competed, drawn by her beauty.
A festive crown was the victor's prize in Greek footraces; here it marks Atalanta's win, not a reward for a suitor.
Atalanta defeats suitors in a footrace; the loser is put to death. Hippomenes has just come to race her.
Cupid is the god of love. Atalanta's first love is the very feeling she has been avoiding by her race rule.
Hippomenes is a descendant of Neptune. Atalanta's father set a race: suitors who lost were put to death, and the winner would marry her.
Venus is invisible to everyone but Hippomenes. Gods in Ovid often intervene unseen in human affairs.

literary_notes.text: The narrator opens with a general reflection on time's swiftness, framing Adonis's rapid growth that follows.
Cupid, who wounds others with love, accidentally wounds his own mother, so love's power turns back on its mistress.
Venus's change from shade-loving beauty to rough huntress shows how love transforms her habits and priorities.
Venus advises courage only against fleeing prey, a neat antithesis that sums up her fearful warning.
Venus breaks off to address Adonis directly, making the narration intimate and flattering while conveying how beautiful Atalanta's body is.
Desire is described as a kindled flame, and Hippomenes' praise feeds it, showing his love growing.
Hippomenes mocked the suitors, yet he now admires the very race he condemned, and speed itself becomes beauty.
Atalanta's blush on white skin is compared to purple hangings tinting a white hall, turning her speed into a visual image.
She denies being moved by his beauty, and then admits she could be, revealing feelings she refuses to recognize.
A run of questions, each starting 'And is it not...', shows her talking herself into admiring him while denying it.
She addresses the absent-minded Hippomenes directly, and wishes she had never been seen by him, which shows her affection.
The narrator steps in to explain her state, noting the paradox that she loves yet does not know it.
The breeze is called not envious and carries the prayer like a messenger, as if the wind had feelings and goodwill.
Exaggeration of the runners' lightness, walking on the sea and the corn, conveys their extraordinary speed.
Atalanta's slowing to look at Hippomenes shows she is already in love and half wants to lose.
The shift to the present tense makes the race feel immediate, even though Venus is narrating a past event.
Venus, the goddess of love, is the one who forces Atalanta to pick up the apple. Love is thus helped by trickery.
